reading.title: Separating process names from equipment
reading.text: The student reads a production vocabulary display. Crushing breaks grape skins; pressing separates juice from solids. Fermentation transforms sugars into alcohol, carbon dioxide and other products. Maceration involves contact between juice and grape solids. Racking transfers liquid away from sediment; fining and filtering are different clarification methods. Aging concerns development during storage, blending combines components, and bottling packages the finished liquid. A wine press is equipment for pressing, and a fermentation tank holds fermenting liquid. An oak barrel is a wooden storage vessel; a stainless steel tank is a metal vessel. A crusher breaks berries. The student asks what a process does before naming its equipment. The display explains distinctions rather than supplies operating instructions, chemical additions or a recipe.

reading.title: Understanding instruments and barrel terms
reading.text: The next display describes a destemmer, which separates berries from stems, and a pump, which moves liquid. A hydrometer measures relative density; a pH meter measures acidity on the pH scale rather than determines every acid's concentration. A corking machine inserts corks. French oak and American oak describe different wood origins and customary barrel materials. Toasting heats the wood, while char refers to a visibly burned surface. New barrel and used barrel concern previous use rather than color alone. Micro-oxidation names a controlled oxygen-introduction technique. Lees are fermentation sediment. Sur lie means keeping wine in contact with those lees; bâtonnage means stirring them. The student checks these distinctions without operating equipment or treating the terminology as an instruction for a production batch.

reading.title: Reading product-category descriptions
reading.text: The student compares category descriptions rather than judges a drink by color alone. Red wine usually obtains color through contact with dark grape skins. White wine generally uses limited skin contact; rosé has a pink appearance from its production method. Sparkling describes carbon dioxide bubbles. Dessert wine names a sweet category, while fortified wine has added distilled spirit. Natural wine is an informal term with varying definitions; it does not guarantee safety, health benefits or universal certification. Orange wine usually uses white grapes with extended skin contact. Ice wine concerns grapes naturally frozen on the vine before pressing, under relevant rules. Port is a protected wine designation associated with Portugal's Douro region and includes different colors and styles. Written records, not a generic bottle photograph, support these classifications.
